title: Computer Vision Fundamentals
learning_outcomes: Explain computer Vision Fundamentals and connect at least two of its listed subtopics.
Apply the central idea in computer Vision Fundamentals to a small example or select a suitable approach for a stated scenario.
Identify an important assumption, failure mode, risk, or limitation and describe how it should be checked.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study computer Vision Fundamentals within Specialized Fields of Artificial Intelligence. You will connect the syllabus topics below to a small, inspectable example and practice stating what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: AI specializations reuse shared foundations but differ in data, output, evaluation, and deployment constraints. Choose a method for a defined use case.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Computer vision maps numerical image representations to tasks such as classification, detection, or segmentation. Resolution, labeling, capture conditions, preprocessing, and subgroup variation affect the reliability of visual predictions.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics covered in this lesson

items.title: Images as numerical arrays
items.text: Images as numerical arrays is one of the concepts used to reason about computer vision fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Image classification
items.text: Image classification is one of the concepts used to reason about computer vision fundamentals. Define the inputs, assumptions, and intended result in this context, then test the idea on a small representative example and document where it may not apply.

items.title: Object detection
items.text: Object detection predicts both class labels and locations for objects in an image. Evaluate localization and classification separately when the use case needs both.

items.title: Image segmentation
items.text: Segmentation assigns labels to pixels or image regions, providing more detailed boundaries than image-level classification. Evaluate with metrics that match the granularity and consequence of errors.

content_blocks.text: 1. Identify what computer vision fundamentals takes as input and what result or decision it is intended to support. 2. content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: If the output differs, check indentation and spelling, confirm you saved the intended file, and compare each input value with the example. If the example runs as expected, do not infer that it proves a trained model works; this snippet is a deterministic teaching aid. Keep sensitive data out of tests.

content_blocks.title: Check before you trust a result
content_blocks.text: This is a small, deterministic teaching example—not a trained AI model or evidence of production performance. Run it with a local Python 3 interpreter; do not paste secrets or private data into experiments.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Computer vision maps numerical image representations to tasks such as classification, detection, or segmentation. Resolution, labeling, capture conditions, preprocessing, and subgroup variation affect the reliability of visual predictions. Next, connect this lesson to its prerequisite or next lesson and carry the same habit forward: define success, test a representative case, inspect failures, and document limitations.

content.task: Try it yourself: choose a small, synthetic example for computer vision fundamentals. Explain the inputs and outputs, compare a simple baseline where appropriate, and write one limitation that should be checked on representative data.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core concept and accurately refer to the source syllabus topics.
Record a prediction and compare it with a reproducible result or a clearly stated manual trace.
Document at least one limitation, safety consideration, or evaluation requirement.
hints: Write down the inputs, expected output, and assumptions before changing the example.
Change only one input or condition and compare the results with your original prediction.
Ask whether the example covers realistic cases, important subgroups, and failure conditions; a toy example does not establish production reliability.
troubleshooting: Use Python 3 and run the file from the folder where it was saved.
If output differs, restore the original input and compare one changed value at a time.
If Python reports a syntax error, check copied quotation marks, indentation, and whether the full code block was copied.
These examples require no external packages, network access, model credentials, or personal data.
